title: Migration 57 — the broker's private note moves out of the supplier's reach
description: Applies migration 57 to the reconciled substrate, runs its VERIFY A-G, then rolls it back. `inventory_batches.owner_notes` is DDP's internal note -- the admin screen labels it 'Internal:' and a trigger exists specifically to stop a farmer WRITING it -- but nothing stopped a farmer READING it, measured on staging 2026-08-05. The fix cannot be a column privilege, and the reason is the interesting part: a DDP admin and a farmer are the SAME PostgreSQL role (`authenticated`), distinguished only by `is_ddp_admin()` inside a row-level policy. Any control at the privilege layer hits both identically. RLS is the only mechanism here that can tell them apart, and RLS is row-level -- so the secret has to live in its own row. Two couplings make this migration more than a column move. The trigger `trg_protect_owner_notes` fires BEFORE UPDATE and assigns NEW.owner_notes, so dropping the column while it is attached breaks every batch update in the platform; it is dropped first and VERIFY G proves updates still work. And `fn_protect_owner_notes()` is deliberately LEFT orphaned, because its body differs between production (the real pin) and the test substrate (a stub), so a rollback re-creating it would have to pick one and be wrong in the other world. NOT read-only; wrapped in BEGIN..ROLLBACK.

verify.note: C is the section that carries the migration, and it asserts in BOTH directions: the farmer who OWNS the batch sees zero note rows, AND still sees the batch itself. Without the second half a farmer who could see nothing at all would pass just as well, and the test would be measuring a broken fixture rather than a working lock. The admin arm is the other control -- a lock nobody can open is not a fix. D exists because a read hole traded for a write hole is no improvement: a farmer able to INSERT a note could plant something in DDP's own record of the batch. G is the regression guard for the dropped trigger, which fired BEFORE UPDATE and assigned a column that no longer exists -- had it been left attached, every batch update in the platform would raise, and no other section would have noticed. NOT PROVEN HERE: that the application stops sending the note to the browser. This closes it at the database, which is the layer a farmer cannot go around; the TypeScript changes ship alongside and are covered by their own tests.
